title: What Happens If You Work More Than 28 Hours on a Student Visa
summary: There is no fine for hour 29. The real mechanism is status cancellation, and the grounds for it are not about hours at all. Here is what the law actually says.
body_html:
The usual question is "what is the fine?" There isn't one. No penalty is attached to the twenty-ninth hour, and looking for one leads you away from what actually happens.

What happens instead runs through two separate pieces of law, and only one of them is about you.

First: the work itself becomes illegal work

The agency defines illegal work as three specific cases. [source:1] The third is working beyond the scope the agency permitted, and the example given for it is a student working more hours than their permit allows. [source:1]

So this is not a grey area or a technicality. Hour 29 is not a slightly-over-the-line version of legal work; it falls inside a defined category with its own name.

That matters because the category, not the hour count, is what everything downstream attaches to.

The famous penalty is not yours

The figure that circulates in forum threads — imprisonment and a large fine — is real, and it is printed on the agency's own leaflet. [source:1]

Read who it applies to. It is the penalty for the offence of enabling illegal work: the person who employed you, or who brokered the arrangement. [source:1] The leaflet is addressed to employers. [source:1]

This gets quoted at students as though it were their sentence. It isn't. Repeating it to yourself produces the wrong kind of fear — fear of a courtroom, when the actual risk is administrative and quieter.

Second: what can actually happen to your status

Your side runs through status cancellation, under Article 22-4, paragraph 1 of the Immigration Act. [source:2] The minister may cancel the status of residence a foreign national currently holds when any of the listed facts is found. [source:2]

Two of the listed grounds are the ones that reach a student who has been working too much. Neither one mentions hours.

Ground 5: holding a status listed in Appended Table I while not carrying out the activity that status is for, and residing in Japan carrying out or intending to carry out some other activity instead — absent a legitimate reason. [source:2] Student status is on that table. [source:2]

Ground 6: not carrying out the activity of that status for 3 months or more running, absent a legitimate reason. [source:2]

Look at what those actually test. Not "did you exceed a number" but "are you still a student". A person who works heavily and keeps attending is in a different position from one who stopped attending, and the grounds are written to capture the second.

This is why the honest answer to "how many hours before something happens" is that hours are the wrong axis. Attendance is the axis.

The procedure is not instant

Before cancellation, an immigration inspector must hear from you. [source:2] You can state your case, submit evidence, and ask to inspect the materials. [source:2]

What follows depends on which ground applied.

  • For grounds 3 through 10 — which includes both grounds above — a period is set for you to leave voluntarily, up to 30 days. [source:2]
  • For ground 5 specifically, if there is reasonable cause to suspect you would abscond, deportation proceedings begin immediately instead. [source:2]
  • If you do not leave within the period set, you become subject to deportation and to criminal penalty. [source:2]

The gap between "30 days to sort yourself out" and "removed immediately" is behaviour during the process, not the original breach. [source:2] That is worth knowing before you decide to avoid a letter from immigration.

The quieter risk nobody warns you about

Cancellation is the dramatic outcome and the rare one. The ordinary one is a renewal that does not go your way.

Your status comes with an expiry, and extending it is a fresh application judged on your circumstances. We are not going to tell you what weight anything carries in that assessment, because the agency does not publish a formula and anyone who claims to know one is guessing.

What we can say is structural: the same facts that would support a cancellation ground — not attending, working instead of studying — are facts about your period of stay, and a renewal application is where your period of stay gets looked at.

Also on that list, and easy to trip over

Grounds 8 and 9 of the same article have nothing to do with work, and catch people who never worked an illegal hour. [source:2] A new mid-to-long-term resident who does not register their address within 90 days of permission can have their status cancelled. [source:2] So can a resident who moves out and does not register the new address within 90 days of leaving the old one. [source:2]

Both have a legitimate-reason exception. [source:2] Neither is worth testing. If you move, register.

What to do

  • Count your hours per week, not per month. The limit is weekly, and averaging across a month is not the same test.
  • If you are already over, the thing to protect is attendance. The grounds that bite are about whether you are still studying. [source:2]
  • Do not keep working while hoping it resolves itself. Ground 6 runs on a 3 month clock. [source:2]
  • If you receive anything from immigration, respond to it. The hearing is your opportunity to submit evidence, and the immediate-deportation route exists for people who look like they are running. [source:2]
  • If your financial situation genuinely does not work at the permitted hours, talk to your school before it becomes an attendance problem. That is a conversation with options; a cancellation hearing is not.

If you have not yet got the permit itself, that is a separate step with a decision in it — see where to apply for the work permit. For what the weekly limit covers and the school-monitoring rules that came in alongside it, see what actually changed about the part-time work rules.

This page summarises published law and agency guidance; it is not legal advice. Individual cases turn on their own facts, and the grounds above all carry legitimate-reason exceptions whose application is decided case by case. [source:2] The sources are linked below. If you are already in difficulty, talk to a lawyer or an administrative scrivener registered with the immigration bureau rather than to a forum.

claims_without_sources: 不法就労助長罪の具体的な量刑（懲役年数・罰金額）—— リーフレットに明記されているが、本文では数字を書かず「懲役と高額の罰金」とだけ述べた。理由は二つ。(1) この記事の要点は金額の大小ではなく「その罰則は雇用主側のものであって学生のものではない」という帰属であり、数字を書くと学生が自分の刑罰だと読む危険がかえって増す。(2) 「300万円」を英文で 3 million yen と書くと闸门の数字抽出が単位を取れず、核対されないまま通る —— 核対されない数字を本文に置かないという原則を、自分の都合で曲げたくない。金額は出典リンクで確認できる。
在留期間更新が不許可になる条件・判断基準 —— 入管庁は更新審査の基準を数値や要件の形で公表していない。したがって「取消事由に該当するような事実は在留状況に関する事実であり、更新申請では在留状況が見られる」という構造的な説明までに留め、「◯時間超えると更新が通らない」といった相場観は一切書いていない。
退去強制事由（入管法第24条）の具体的な号 —— 退去強制手続のページは第24条に該当する旨を述べるが号の列挙はしておらず、条文そのものを出典として確認していないため、号番号を書いていない。
週の起算日（月曜起算か、学校の定めるところか）—— 入管庁の公表資料に記載を見つけられなかった。「週あたりで数えよ」とだけ書き、起算日は示していない。
資格外活動許可を取り消される（許可自体の撤回）という扱いの有無 —— 在留資格の取消しとは別の制度であり、公表資料から確認できなかったため触れていない。
